questions.prompt: Complete: "Before the bypass was built, this street ___ much quieter than it is today."

options.text: is used to be
use to be
used to be
used to being

questions.explanation: A state that belonged to the past and has stopped takes used to followed by the base verb, which gives "used to be". "use to be" drops the -d that carries the past. "is used to be" brings in be used to, a present state meaning accustomed to, and that structure never takes a base verb. "used to being" borrows the -ing form that belongs to be used to.

questions.prompt: The programme offered three workshops, and the one on robotics drew the biggest crowd of the three. Which sentence says so?

options.text: The robotics workshop was more popular.
The robotics workshop was the most popular.
The robotics workshop was the popularest.
The robotics workshop was most popular than the others.

questions.explanation: One item placed at the top of a whole group takes the superlative, and a long adjective builds it with the most: "The robotics workshop was the most popular." "The robotics workshop was more popular." is a comparative and leaves you asking: more popular than what? "The robotics workshop was the popularest." adds -est to an adjective that is far too long for that ending. "The robotics workshop was most popular than the others." mixes a superlative with than, which belongs to a comparative.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The lifts ___ while the engineers are working on the roof."

options.text: cannot be used
cannot be using
cannot to be used
cannot used

questions.explanation: After a modal the passive has a fixed shape, modal + be + past participle, so the lifts "cannot be used". "cannot be using" keeps an active -ing form, which would make the lifts the ones doing the using. "cannot used" drops be, and without be there is no passive at all. "cannot to be used" slips the to of the infinitive after a modal, which never takes one.

questions.prompt: Amel said: "My father repaired my bike." Which report of her words is correct?

options.text: Amel said that my father had repaired my bike.
Amel said that her father had repaired my bike.
Amel said that his father had repaired her bike.
Amel said that her father had repaired her bike.

questions.explanation: When you report somebody's words, every my of the speaker becomes her, and Amel says my twice, so both become her: "Amel said that her father had repaired her bike." "Amel said that my father had repaired my bike." leaves the two possessives with the speaker, so the sentence claims that the bike and the father are yours. "Amel said that her father had repaired my bike." shifts only the first of the two. "Amel said that his father had repaired her bike." makes the father somebody else's.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences can take the words "in 2004" at the end without any other change?

options.text: The association changed its name.
The association has changed its name.
The association has been open since then.
The association has never changed its name.

questions.explanation: A moment named and finished goes only with the simple past, so the sentence that accepts in 2004 is "The association changed its name." The three others are present perfects, and the present perfect refuses a moment named in the sentence: "The association has changed its name." gives a result without saying when, "The association has been open since then." already carries its own starting point, and "The association has never changed its name." says the change never happened, so no date can be attached to it.
